All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

Solving $AJ+JA^{T}=0$ blockwise gives
$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&u&-w^{T}\\ w&a&b\\ -u^{T}&c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix},\qquad u\in M_{1\times n}(\mathbb C),\quad w\in M_{n\times1}(\mathbb C),\quad b,c\ \text{skew-symmetric},$$
for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$. In particular
$\dim\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n+1)=\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$
and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the
bracket: if $AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$, then
$[A,B]J+J[A,B]^{T}=ABJ-BAJ+JB^{T}A^{T}-JA^{T}B^{T}$, and substituting
$AJ=-JA^{T}$ and $BJ=-JB^{T}$ (equivalently $JA^{T}=-AJ$ and $JB^{T}=-BJ$) makes
the four terms cancel in pairs. For $n\ge1$, each symplectic or orthogonal family is a nonzero proper subspace of
$M_m(\mathbb C)$ closed under the commutator, hence a Lie subalgebra.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, let $G$
be a connected smooth algebraic group scheme of finite type over $k$ (such a
$G$ is separated by Milne 1.22 and geometrically reduced, hence a classical
variety of finite type over $k$) acting on a classical variety $X$ over $k$
([[def-dimension-classical-variety]],
[[cor-smooth-variety-classical-scheme-conventions-agree]]), and let
$x\in X(k)$ be a closed point. Then: (a) every fibre over a closed $k$-point of
the orbit map $\varrho_x:G\to O_x$ is a left translate of the stabilizer $G_x$
([[lem-action-map-fibres-and-stabilizer-subscheme]]), hence has underlying
topological dimension $\dim G_x$, equivalently the dimension of its reduction;
$G_x$ may be nonreduced ([[def-dimension-noetherian-topological-space]]);
(b) $\dim G=\dim G_x+\dim O_x$; (c) the orbit closure $\overline{O_x}$ is the
union of $O_x$ and of orbits of strictly smaller dimension; consequently every
orbit of minimal dimension in $X$ is closed, and $\overline{O_x}$ contains a
closed orbit. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the generic-fibre and
constructibility inputs.

after_value.claim: **Empty chains.** If $V=0$, take $t=0$; if $e=0$ on a nonzero space, its Jordan diagram has a single column and $t=1$. In either case there are no chain variables or equations, $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ is trivial and $\theta=0$. Its image is the point orbit closure, its coordinate ring is a normal domain, and the empty equation sequence is regular. The boundary is empty and has codimension $+\infty$. All conclusions follow in these cases. Henceforth $t\ge2$.

**The open chain locus.** Put $c=\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$ and $D=2\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-c$. The differential of the chain equations is $Y_iA_i+B_iX_i-X_{i-1}B_{i-1}-A_{i-1}Y_{i-1}$, with the index-zero terms zero. If each $A_i$ is injective or $B_i$ is surjective, these equations can be solved successively for any prescribed right-hand sides: use a left inverse of $A_i$ to choose $Y_i$, or a right inverse of $B_i$ to choose $X_i$, after the preceding pair is fixed. Thus the open locus $Z^\circ$ with this condition is smooth of dimension $D$ by [F4]. It is nonempty: use $U_i=\operatorname{im}e^{t-i}$, inclusions $A_i$, and restrictions $B_i=e|_{U_{i+1}}$, transported to the fixed spaces. These maps satisfy the equations and have end map $e$.

**Alternating strings and their stabilizers.** For a nilpotent pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, the odd operator $T$ on $U\oplus W$ with these components has a homogeneous Jordan-string decomposition: kernels and images of its powers are graded, so the complements in the Jordan construction may be chosen homogeneous. Every string alternates letters $a$ from $U$ and $b$ from $W$. Removing all $b$ letters gives the Jordan rows of $BA$, and removing all $a$ letters gives those of $AB$. The ranks of alternating composites recover the numbers of strings of each length and starting letter, so a diagram determines one pair orbit and there are finitely many diagrams in fixed dimensions. The pair stabilizer is the unit group of its even endomorphism algebra, an open subset of a vector space and hence smooth and irreducible. On a string $A$ kills exactly a terminal $a$ and $B$ misses exactly an initial $a$; consequently $A$ is injective iff every string ends in $b$, and $B$ is surjective iff every string begins in $b$.

**Even orbit drops.** Distinct dominated types have strictly smaller orbit dimension. One can move from a dominating partition to a dominated one by repeatedly moving a box from an earlier row to a later allowable row: choose an excess row and a subsequent deficit row, taking the last row of the source plateau and the first allowed destination to preserve the partition inequalities, and repeat until the target is reached. A move from row $i$ to row $j>i$ increases $\sum_r(2r-1)\mu_r$ by $2(j-i)$ and therefore decreases the orbit dimension by that positive even number. Each allowable unit move from row lengths $a,b$ with $a\ge b+2$ is realized by a one-parameter degeneration. On chains $u_1,\ldots,u_{a-1}$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_{b+1}$ of the destination type, keep the usual lowering maps except send $v_{b+1}$ to $v_b+z u_{a-1}$, with $v_0=0$. At $z=0$ the type is $(a-1,b+1)$; for $z\ne0$ the ranks of powers are those of $(a,b)$ (the chain generated by $v_{b+1}$ has length $a$, and the remaining chain has length $b$). Keeping other strings fixed proves that dominated types belong to the top orbit closure. Hence a drop of exactly two consists of one box moved to the next row; any other drop is at least four. Equivalently, parity also follows from $\sum_j(\mu'_j)^2\equiv\sum_j\mu'_j=N\pmod2$ for the total sum; individual summands in a difference of square sums need not be even.

**The pair-orbit dimension.** Write $m=\dim U$, $n=\dim W$, and let $E,O$ be the dimensions of the even and odd centralizers of $T$. A homomorphism between Jordan strings of lengths $L,L'$ has $\min(L,L')$ possible shifts. Counting the parity of those shifts, odd strings of the same endpoint type contribute $+1$ to the even-minus-odd count, and odd strings of opposite type contribute $-1$; the two opposite Hom directions for an odd/even pair cancel, and even/even pairs contribute zero. Summing gives $E-O=(m-n)^2$, because the difference between the numbers of odd $a$-type and odd $b$-type strings is $m-n$. The pair orbit therefore has dimension $m^2+n^2-E=\tfrac12((m+n)^2-E-O)$, half the dimension of the ordinary orbit of $T$. If a string has $r_j$ letters $a$ and $s_j$ letters $b$, then $\min(r_j+s_j,r_k+s_k)=\min(r_j,r_k)+\min(s_j,s_k)$ except for equal odd lengths with opposite endpoint types, where the left side is larger by one. Let $a_l,b_l$ count the odd strings of length $l$ beginning with the two respective letters, and put $\Delta=\sum_{l\text{ odd}}a_lb_l$. The ordinary Jordan centralizer counts now give $\dim O_{(A,B)}=mn+\tfrac12(\dim C_{BA}+\dim C_{AB})-\Delta$. This is a dimension identity for the orbit, not for the full matrix space minus the pair orbit.

**Chain strata.** Stratify $Z$ by its compatible alternating-string diagrams at every link. Compatibility means that the $b$-diagram of one link equals the $a$-diagram of the next. These are finitely many locally closed strata. Pair-orbit projections to either ordinary Jordan orbit are smooth homogeneous fibrations: their fibers are quotients of the ordinary centralizer unit group by the pair stabilizer. Both groups are smooth connected open subsets of finite-dimensional endomorphism spaces, so these fibers are irreducible. Iterating these fibrations proves each nonempty chain stratum $Z_\delta$ smooth and irreducible. The dimension at each fiber-product step is the preceding dimension plus the pair-orbit dimension minus the shared Jordan-orbit dimension. The intermediate orbit dimensions cancel in the formula of step 2.1, giving $\dim Z_\delta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12\dim C_\sigma-\sum_{i<t}\Delta_i$, where $\sigma$ is the type of its final end map.

**Dominance and the top stratum.** The chain equations make $\theta^k$ factor through $U_{t-k}$, so $\operatorname{rank}\theta^k\le n_{t-k}$ and $\theta^t=0$. Thus its type $\sigma$ is dominated by $\eta$ by [F3]. For a $b$-diagram $\sigma$, every row must first be filled internally by alternating $a$ letters; this requires exactly $|\sigma|-\ell(\sigma)$ letters, the size of the diagram obtained by deleting its first column. Over the top diagram $\eta$, this equals $n_{t-1}$, leaving no extra letters: every string starts and ends in $b$ and the lower diagram is exactly the first-column deletion of $\eta$. Repeat down the chain. There is exactly one top stratum; it has both maximal-rank maps at every link, lies in $Z^\circ$, and has every $\Delta_i=0$. Finally, expanding $q_j=n_{t-j+1}-n_{t-j}$ gives $\tfrac12\dim C_\eta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$, so its dimension is $D$.

**Drops of at least four.** By the stratum formula and the nonnegativity of all $\Delta_i$, a final orbit drop of at least four gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-4)=D-2$. Every non-top stratum has dimension at most $D-1$. This latter estimate establishes uniqueness of the dense top stratum but does not assert that every non-top stratum has codimension two: some are smooth divisors inside $Z^\circ$.

**Drops of two and the nonsmooth-locus bound.** Suppose $\sigma$ is obtained from $\eta$ by moving a box to the next row. Let $\eta'$ and $\sigma'$ denote first-column deletions and let $m=|\eta'|$, $m'=|\sigma'|$. At the last link the available number of $a$ letters is $m$ and its $a$-diagram must be dominated by $\eta'$, since its powers factor through the shorter chain. If the receiving row was nonempty, $m=m'$: internal filling consumes every $a$, all strings begin and end in $b$, and the same next-row degeneration passes to the shorter chain. If a new singleton row is created, $m=m'+1$. After internal filling there is one extra $a$. It can be attached at either end of the shortened last row, at either end of the new singleton $b$ row, or placed in a new singleton $a$ row. No earlier row can receive it: its $a$-diagram would gain a box earlier than the removed last-row box and violate dominance by $\eta'$. In the first four placements one map is maximal rank; the lower diagram is either $\eta'$ or its next-row degeneration. In the fifth placement both maps fail maximal rank, and singleton strings of both types occur, giving $\Delta_i\ge1$. This remains valid when the shortened row is itself a singleton, when there can be more than one singleton $b$. Inducting through the shorter chain shows that either every link has a maximal-rank map and $Z_\delta\subseteq Z^\circ$, or some $\Delta_i\ge1$. In the latter case the dimension formula gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-2)-1=D-2$. Together with step 5.1, this proves $\dim(Z\setminus Z^\circ)\le D-2$.

**Complete intersection and reducedness.** Every irreducible component of the scheme cut out by its $c$ equations has dimension at least $\dim M-c=D$ by [F4]. The top stratum has dimension $D$ and all other strata have smaller dimension by step 5.1, so every component has dimension $D$. Thus the equation ideal has height $c$. Its homogeneous generators form a regular sequence in the polynomial ring: at the homogeneous maximal ideal, every prefix of length $k$ has height at least $k$, since adjoining the remaining $c-k$ equations raises height by at most $c-k$; the opposite inequality is Krull's bound. Complete the generators to a system of parameters and apply the Cohen-Macaulay parameter theorem in [F4]. Homogeneous localization detects a kernel in a multiplication map, so regularity is global. The quotient is Cohen-Macaulay, hence satisfies $S_1$ and $S_2$. Every component meets the smooth open $Z^\circ$ by step 6.1, so it satisfies $R_0$; [F5] implies reducedness.

**Irreducibility and normality of the chain.** The unique top stratum is irreducible. before_value.claim: Hartogs lifting. Let $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and let $f\in\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ be regular on $O$, hence regular off a closed subset of $X\setminus O$; since $\partial X$ has codimension $\ge2$ in $X$ by the normality lemma [F1], $f$ is regular in codimension $1$ and therefore extends to $A$ by [F2]. Applying this coordinatewise to maps into a finite-dimensional vector space shows that every regular map $O\to W$ into a finite-dimensional vector space extends uniquely to a regular map $X\to W$.

The equivariant map on $O$. Fix $B\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})^{G_e}$ and define, for $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $F(g\,e\,g^{-1}):=(g^{\otimes d})\,B\,(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. This is well defined: if $g_1e g_1^{-1}=g_2eg_2^{-1}$, then $g_2^{-1}g_1\in G_e$, so $(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{\otimes d}B(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{-\otimes d}=B$ by $G_e$-invariance, which rearranges to $(g_1^{\otimes d})B(g_1^{-1})^{\otimes d}=(g_2^{\otimes d})B(g_2^{-1})^{\otimes d}$. The map $F$ is $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant by construction: $F(hXh^{-1})=(h^{\otimes d})F(X)(h^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ for $X\in O$.

Regularity of $F$ on $O$. The ranks of $X^0,X^1,\dots,X^{l-1}$ are constant on $O$. Cover $O$ by open charts where fixed minors used to select bases of the kernels and images, their quotient complements and Jordan top vectors are nonzero. Gaussian elimination on such a chart gives a Jordan basis for $X$ with entries regular in $X$. Let $g(X)$ carry a fixed Jordan basis for $e$ to this chosen Jordan basis for $X$, with the same ordered string lengths. Then $g(X)e g(X)^{-1}=X$. Restricting to the open chart where the Jordan-basis determinant is nonzero makes both $g(X)$ and $g(X)^{-1}$ regular, since their entries have only the fixed nonvanishing minors and determinant as denominators. Thus $X\mapsto(g(X)^{\otimes d})B(g(X)^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ is the map of step 1.2 and is regular on each chart. These charts cover $O$; on overlaps $g_2(X)^{-1}g_1(X)\in G_e$, so the expressions agree by $G_e$-invariance of $B$. Hence $F$ is regular on $O$.

Extension to $X$. By steps 1.2 and 2.1 the map $F\colon O\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ is a regular equivariant map on the dense orbit; by step 1.1 it extends uniquely to a regular map $F\colon X\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. Since $\mathbb C[X]=\mathbb C[\operatorname{End}(V)]/I(X)$ and $X$ is an affine closed subset of the affine space $\operatorname{End}(V)$, the coordinate functions of $F$ are restrictions of polynomial functions on $\operatorname{End}(V)$; fixing representatives gives a polynomial map $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ extending $F$.

Equivariance of $\Phi$. For fixed $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, both sides of $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ are polynomial maps in $X$; they agree on the dense orbit $O$ by step 1.2 and hence on all of $X$. Consequently the class of $\Phi$ in the finite-dimensional space of polynomial maps $\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ of degree at most $K$ (for $K$ at least the degree of $\Phi$), modulo the $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-stable subspace of maps vanishing on $X$, is invariant for the conjugation action. By the invariant-lifting property of complete reducibility [F3], this class has an invariant representative $\Phi'$ of degree at most $K$; then $\Phi'$ is a $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant polynomial map on $\operatorname{End}(V)$ agreeing with $F$ on $X$, and $\Phi'(e)=F(e)=B$ since $e\in O$, which is assertion (1).

Polarization. Write $\Phi=\sum_k\Phi_k$ for its homogeneous components of degree $k$; each $\Phi_k$ is equivariant. Fix $k$ and assume for the structure argument that $\Phi$ is homogeneous of degree $k$. Polarize the $k$ matrix variables $X_1,\dots,X_k$ of $\Phi$ and pair the output in $\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ with $d$ independent matrices $Y_1,\dots,Y_d$ using the nondegenerate trace pairing on each tensor factor; this produces a multilinear $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-invariant $P(X_1,\dots,X_k;Y_1,\dots,Y_d)\in\mathbb C$ in $(k+d)$ matrix arguments.

Tensor invariants are permutation contractions. By the Schur-Weyl description [F3], every multilinear invariant of the matrix arguments is a linear combination of contractions: each argument contributes one upper and one lower index, an invariant pairs each upper index with a lower index of another argument, and the invariant is a product over the cycles of the resulting permutation of traces of the corresponding cyclically ordered product of matrices.

Covariant normal form. Depolarize in the $k$ identical variables $X_i=X$ and read each contraction cycle. A cycle that uses only $X$-arguments contributes a scalar invariant polynomial in $X$; a cycle that uses some $Y$-arguments alternates blocks of $X$'s and single $Y$'s, so its trace is precisely the trace pairing of $Y_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Y_d$ with a place permutation of $X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d}$. By nondegeneracy of the trace pairing, the operator identity $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ follows, with $h_i\ge0$, $\sigma_h$ a place permutation and $c_h$ a scalar invariant polynomial (a polynomial in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^m)$); summing over the homogeneous components gives assertion (2).

Evaluation at $e$. Since $e^l=0$ for the largest Jordan block length $l$ of $e$, evaluating the normal form at $X=e$ kills every term with some $h_i\ge l$; the surviving terms are place permutations applied to a tensor product of nonnegative powers $e^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{h_d}$ multiplied by the scalar invariants $c_h(e)$, which are ordinary numbers depending only on the Jordan type of $e$ (that is, on the list of eigenvalues $\operatorname{tr}(e^m)$, all zero for nilpotent $e$, so $c_h(e)=c_h(0)$). This gives the concrete description of the $G_e$-fixed endomorphisms used by the double centralizer theorem.

Applying this coordinatewise to maps into a finite-dimensional vector space shows that every regular map $O\to W$ into a finite-dimensional vector space extends uniquely to a regular map $X\to W$.

The equivariant map on $O$. Fix $B\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})^{G_e}$ and define, for $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $F(g\,e\,g^{-1}):=(g^{\otimes d})\,B\,(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. This is well defined: if $g_1e g_1^{-1}=g_2eg_2^{-1}$, then $g_2^{-1}g_1\in G_e$, so $(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{\otimes d}B(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{-\otimes d}=B$ by $G_e$-invariance, which rearranges to $(g_1^{\otimes d})B(g_1^{-1})^{\otimes d}=(g_2^{\otimes d})B(g_2^{-1})^{\otimes d}$. The map $F$ is $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant by construction: $F(hXh^{-1})=(h^{\otimes d})F(X)(h^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ for $X\in O$.

Regularity of $F$ on $O$. The ranks of $X^0,X^1,\dots,X^{l-1}$ are constant on $O$. Cover $O$ by open charts where fixed minors used to select bases of the kernels and images, their quotient complements and Jordan top vectors are nonzero. Gaussian elimination on such a chart gives a Jordan basis for $X$ with entries regular in $X$. Let $g(X)$ carry a fixed Jordan basis for $e$ to this chosen Jordan basis for $X$, with the same ordered string lengths. Then $g(X)e g(X)^{-1}=X$. Restricting to the open chart where the Jordan-basis determinant is nonzero makes both $g(X)$ and $g(X)^{-1}$ regular, since their entries have only the fixed nonvanishing minors and determinant as denominators. Thus $X\mapsto(g(X)^{\otimes d})B(g(X)^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ is the map of step 1.3 and is regular on each chart. These charts cover $O$; on overlaps $g_2(X)^{-1}g_1(X)\in G_e$, so the expressions agree by $G_e$-invariance of $B$. Hence $F$ is regular on $O$.

Extension to $X$. By steps 1.2 and 2.1 the map $F\colon O\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ is a regular equivariant map on the dense orbit; by step 1.2 it extends uniquely to a regular map $F\colon X\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. Since $\mathbb C[X]=\mathbb C[\operatorname{End}(V)]/I(X)$ and $X$ is an affine closed subset of the affine space $\operatorname{End}(V)$, the coordinate functions of $F$ are restrictions of polynomial functions on $\operatorname{End}(V)$; fixing representatives gives a polynomial map $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ extending $F$.

Equivariance of $\Phi$. For fixed $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, both sides of $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ are polynomial maps in $X$; they agree on the dense orbit $O$ by step 1.3 and hence on all of $X$. Polarization. Write $\Phi=\sum_k\Phi_k$ for its homogeneous components of degree $k$; each $\Phi_k$ is equivariant. Fix $k$ and assume for the structure argument that $\Phi$ is homogeneous of degree $k$. Polarize the $k$ matrix variables $X_1,\dots,X_k$ of $\Phi$ and pair the output in $\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ with $d$ independent matrices $Y_1,\dots,Y_d$ using the nondegenerate trace pairing on each tensor factor; this produces a multilinear $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-invariant $P(X_1,\dots,X_k;Y_1,\dots,Y_d)\in\mathbb C$ in $(k+d)$ matrix arguments.

Tensor invariants are permutation contractions. By the Schur-Weyl description [F3], every multilinear invariant of the matrix arguments is a linear combination of contractions: each argument contributes one upper and one lower index, an invariant pairs each upper index with a lower index of another argument, and the invariant is a product over the cycles of the resulting permutation of traces of the corresponding cyclically ordered product of matrices.

Covariant normal form. Depolarize in the $k$ identical variables $X_i=X$ and read each contraction cycle. A cycle that uses only $X$-arguments contributes a scalar invariant polynomial in $X$; a cycle that uses some $Y$-arguments alternates blocks of $X$'s and single $Y$'s, so its trace is precisely the trace pairing of $Y_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Y_d$ with a place permutation of $X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d}$. By nondegeneracy of the trace pairing, the operator identity $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ follows, with $h_i\ge0$, $\sigma_h$ a place permutation and $c_h$ a scalar invariant polynomial (a polynomial in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^m)$); summing over the homogeneous components gives assertion (2).

Evaluation at $e$. Since $e^l=0$ for the largest Jordan block length $l$ of $e$, evaluating the normal form at $X=e$ kills every term with some $h_i\ge l$; the surviving terms are place permutations applied to a tensor product of nonnegative powers $e^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{h_d}$ multiplied by the scalar invariants $c_h(e)$, which are ordinary numbers depending only on the Jordan type of $e$ (that is, on the list of eigenvalues $\operatorname{tr}(e^m)$, all zero for nilpotent $e$, so $c_h(e)=c_h(0)$). This gives the concrete description of the $G_e$-fixed endomorphisms used by the double centralizer theorem.
